---
title: "Writing a SPEC: data lines, analyses, study data and figures"
---

```{r, include = FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(collapse = TRUE, comment = "#>")
knitr::opts_template$set(code = list(comment = "", class.output = "r"))
options(knitr.kable.NA = "")
```

This article gathers the rules for writing a report SPEC in four parts:
the data lines, the analysis items, the study's data and figures. Each
rule comes with a short YAML example and the R code tflspec writes from
it. The data is the package's fictional example data (`adsl`, `adae`,
`adlb`, `adtte`).

## A study to work in

The examples run in one small study. `tfl_ai_study_init()` writes its
`study.yml` (the datasets and the populations) and
`spec/defaults.yml`.

```{r, message = FALSE}
library(tflspec)

study <- file.path(tempdir(), "rules-study")
dir.create(file.path(study, "adam"), recursive = TRUE, showWarnings = FALSE)
for (x in c("adsl", "adae", "adlb", "adtte")) {
  saveRDS(get(x), file.path(study, "adam", paste0(x, ".rds")))
}
invisible(tfl_ai_study_init(study, adam = "adam", study_id = "RULES-1"))
outputs <- file.path(study, "spec", "outputs")
```

Most examples name a template of the `tflspec_v1` series. One helper
does the same steps for each report. It fills the template in
(`tfl_template_resolve()`), saves the report in the study, and returns
the ARD program (`tfl_ard_code()`) and the ARD it makes
(`tfl_build_ard()`). A second helper prints one section of a program.

```{r}
ard_program <- function(file) {
  out <- tfl_template_resolve(file, study = file.path(study, "study.yml"))
  tfl_write_output(out, file.path(outputs, basename(file)))
  st <- tfl_read_study_spec(study)
  list(spec = out,
       code = tfl_ard_code(st, output_id = out$id, save = FALSE, part = "body"),
       ard = tfl_build_ard(st, dir = study, output_id = out$id, save = FALSE))
}

# the lines of one "# ---- <name> ----" section of a program
section <- function(code, name) {
  code <- unlist(strsplit(code, "\n", fixed = TRUE))
  heads <- grep("^# ---- ", code)
  from <- grep(paste0("^# ---- ", name, " ----"), code)
  to <- c(heads[heads > from], length(code) + 1L)[[1L]] - 1L
  code[from:to]
}
```

## 1. Data lines

A report's `data:` is a list of data lines. Each line makes one named
data set in the ARD program (`adsl_sub`, `adlb_sub` ...). Its keys run in
a fixed order: `from`, the subjects (`population` or `subjects`), the
records `where` keeps, the columns `add` brings from the subjects' data,
`derive`, `keep` and `distinct`.

### `then:` is R at the end of the line

`then:` is R that is piped onto the end of the line's data. It runs after
all the other keys (and after the code lists' levels). It is written as
it stands. The data is its first argument, and it may be a pipe of
several steps.

A line with `code:` cannot have `then:`. `code:` makes the whole data
itself, so there is no end to pipe onto.

### A report line with `code:` replaces the template's line

A report on a template may write a data line with the id of one of the
template's lines. The two are then put together:

- A report line **without** `code:` is merged key by key. The report's
  keys replace the template's keys of the same name. The template's
  other keys stay.
- A report line **with** `code:` replaces the template's line whole.
  None of the template's keys stay. Give the line its `from` too.

Here a demographics report keeps the template's analyses but makes the
subjects' data with its own R:

```{cat, engine.opts = list(file = file.path(tempdir(), "T-1.yml"), lang = "yaml")}
id: T-1
kind: table
label: Demographics, adult subjects
data:
  - id: adsl_sub
    from: ADSL
    code: !r 'adsl |> dplyr::filter(SAFFL == "Y", AGE >= 18)'
template:
  name: tflspec_v1/demog
  analysis:
    by: TRT01A
    continuous: [AGE]
    categorical: [SEX, RACE]
    analysis_ids: {AGE: AGE_STATS}
```

```{r, message = FALSE, opts.label = "code"}
dm <- ard_program(file.path(tempdir(), "T-1.yml"))
cat(section(dm$code, "data"), sep = "\n")
```

The template's line had `population: SAF`. The report's line replaced
it, so the program has only the report's R.

### The Lab template's `record_where`

The `tflspec_v1/lab_tox_shift` template counts each subject's worst
record of a lab test. It does not compute the worst record. It keeps the
records its param `record_where` keeps, in the `adlb_sub` line's
`where`. The default is `AVISIT == "WORST POST-BASELINE"`: the ADaM's own
worst record.

For an ADaM with no worst record, set `record_where` to the records to
choose from, and pick the worst one with `then:` on the template's
`adlb_sub` line. The report line has no `code:`, so it is merged key by
key: the template's `from`, `subjects` and `add` stay.

```{cat, engine.opts = list(file = file.path(tempdir(), "T-4.yml"), lang = "yaml")}
id: T-4
kind: table
label: Shift in toxicity grade, baseline to worst
data:
  - id: adlb_sub
    then: !r 'dplyr::slice_max(dplyr::coalesce(ATOXGRH, ATOXGRL), n = 1, with_ties = FALSE, by = c(USUBJID, PARAMCD))'
template:
  name: tflspec_v1/lab_tox_shift
  data:
    record_where: !r AVISIT != "WORST POST-BASELINE" & is.na(ABLFL)
  analysis:
    by: TRT01A
    conditions:
      - {tox_dir: High, param: Alanine Aminotransferase (U/L)}
      - {tox_dir: Low, param: Hemoglobin (g/L)}
```

```{r, message = FALSE, opts.label = "code"}
lab <- ard_program(file.path(tempdir(), "T-4.yml"))
cat(section(lab$code, "data"), sep = "\n")
```

The `filter()` comes from `record_where`; the `slice_max()` is the
`then:`, last. The grades are in `ATOXGRH` for an upper limit test and in
`ATOXGRL` for a lower limit test, so `dplyr::coalesce()` takes the one
the test has. (`is.na(ABLFL)` and not `ABLFL != "Y"`: the programs read
blanks as `NA`. See part 3.)

## 2. Analysis items

### `analyses: {per, ids}`

A template's analysis item is one block of the SPEC. Its `analyses:` key
says how many analyses it makes, and their ids (`analysis_id`):

| `analyses:` | the analyses | their ids |
|---|---|---|
| no `per` | one | the item's `id` |
| `per: variable` | one a variable | the variable's name, or its entry in `ids` |
| `per: level` | one a depth of a hierarchy | `<id>_ANY`, `<id>_L1`, `<id>_L2` ... |
| `per: [columns]` | one a condition row | the columns' values joined by `_`, upper case |

`ids` gives an analysis its own id. In the demographics template it is
the param `analysis_ids` (above, `{AGE: AGE_STATS}`):

```{r, echo = FALSE, comment = ""}
tpl <- function(name) {
  readLines(system.file("series", "tflspec_v1", "templates", paste0(name, ".yml"),
                        package = "tflspec"))
}
x <- tpl("demog")
cat(x[grep("id: CONT", x, fixed = TRUE) + 0:1], sep = "\n")
```

```{r}
unique(dm$ard$analysis_id)
```

The adverse event template counts by depth. `AE_ANY` is any event,
`AE_L1` the body systems, `AE_L2` the preferred terms:

```{r, echo = FALSE, comment = ""}
x <- tpl("ae_soc_pt")
cat(x[grep("id: AE$", x) + 0:1], sep = "\n")
```

```{cat, engine.opts = list(file = file.path(tempdir(), "T-2.yml"), lang = "yaml")}
id: T-2
kind: table
label: Treatment-emergent adverse events
template:
  name: tflspec_v1/ae_soc_pt
  analysis:
    by: TRT01A
```

```{r, message = FALSE, opts.label = "code"}
ae <- ard_program(file.path(tempdir(), "T-2.yml"))
code <- section(ae$code, "analyses")
cat(code[grep("^# AE: each depth", code):length(code)], sep = "\n")
```

```{r}
unique(ae$ard$analysis_id)
```

The Lab template makes one analysis a condition row: a test and a
direction. Its id is `<PARAMCD>_<TOX_DIR>`, from the data's own
`PARAMCD` and the row's `tox_dir`:

```{r, echo = FALSE, comment = ""}
x <- tpl("lab_tox_shift")
cat(x[grep("id: SHIFT", x, fixed = TRUE) + 0:1], sep = "\n")
```

```{r}
unique(lab$ard$analysis_id)
```

A condition row may give its own `analysis_id`. That id is then used
instead.

### BIGN

Each report has one `BIGN` analysis: the subjects of each column. It is
the column header's N, and the denominator of the percentages. The
templates write it first, on the data their `denominator` param names
(`adsl_sub` by default):

```{r, echo = FALSE, comment = ""}
x <- tpl("ae_soc_pt")
i <- grep("id: BIGN", x, fixed = TRUE)
cat(x[i:(i + 5L)], sep = "\n")
```

The other items say `denominator: BIGN`. In the program that is BIGN's
data, so the percentages and the header N count the same subjects:

```{r, opts.label = "code"}
code <- section(ae$code, "analyses")
cat(code[2:7], grep("denominator", code, value = TRUE), sep = "\n")
```

```{r}
bign <- ae$ard[ae$ard$analysis_id == "BIGN" & ae$ard$stat_name == "n", ]
data.frame(arm = unlist(bign$variable_level), N = unlist(bign$stat))
```

## 3. Study data: `study$adam` and `study$adam_org`

The study's setup file is sourced by every program.
`tfl_study_setup_code()` writes it. It reads each dataset in two
versions, each when it is first used:

- `study$adam_org`: the dataset as the file has it.
- `study$adam`: the same dataset with blanks as `NA` (`blank_as_na()`),
  then the levels of the columns the study's ADaM metadata maps
  (`set_levels()`).

The generated ARD, listing and figure programs always read `study$adam`.
`study$adam_org` is there for a program a person writes on the data as
the file has it. A program run without the setup file reads the files
itself, in the same way (blanks as `NA`, then the levels). Here is the
Lab report's program from part 1:

```{r, opts.label = "code"}
cat(section(lab$code, "input data"), sep = "\n")
```

The levels come from the study's ADaM metadata, `spec/defaults.yml`'s
`adam_meta:` (the rows of a Define-XML: `variables` maps a dataset's
column to a code list, `codelists` gives each list's values in order).
Here it maps ADSL's `SEX`:

```{r}
cat("adam_meta:",
    "  variables:",
    "    - {dataset: ADSL, variable: SEX, codelist: CL.SEX}",
    "  codelists:",
    "    - {codelist: CL.SEX, value: F, decode: Female, order: 1}",
    "    - {codelist: CL.SEX, value: M, decode: Male, order: 2}",
    file = file.path(study, "spec", "defaults.yml"), sep = "\n", append = TRUE)
```

```{r, opts.label = "code"}
setup <- tfl_study_setup_code(tfl_read_study_spec(study))
cat(setup, sep = "\n")
```

The setup's functions come from the study's helpers
(`tfl_helpers_code()`). Run both, and compare the two versions of ADLB:

```{r}
env <- new.env()
old <- setwd(study)
eval(parse(text = tfl_helpers_code()), env)
eval(parse(text = setup), env)
lb_org <- env$study$adam_org$adlb   # (read here, when first used)
lb <- env$study$adam$adlb
sl <- env$study$adam$adsl
setwd(old)

table(lb_org$ABLFL, useNA = "ifany")   # as read: "" and "Y"
table(lb$ABLFL, useNA = "ifany")       # blanks as NA
levels(sl$SEX)                         # CL.SEX's values, in order
```

So a condition on a blank is written `is.na(ABLFL)`, not `ABLFL == ""`.

### `adam_levels: codelists | none`

`study.yml`'s `settings: adam_levels` says whether `study$adam` gets the
levels of `adam_meta`:

- `codelists` (the default, also when the key is not there): blanks as
  `NA`, then the levels of the columns `adam_meta` maps.
- `none`: blanks as `NA` only.

```{r, opts.label = "code"}
y <- file.path(study, "study.yml")
writeLines(sub("^settings:$", "settings:\n  adam_levels: none", readLines(y)), y)
cat(tfl_study_setup_code(tfl_read_study_spec(study)), sep = "\n")
```

The setting is part of each ARD's fingerprint, so changing it marks the
ARD outdated. Under `none`, a report's own levels and labels still work.

## 4. Figures: `figure: {name, args}`

A figure report may name its content as a figure content function. The
code SPEC key is `figure:`, with the function's `name` and its `args`.
There are two functions:

- `fig_km`: the Kaplan-Meier figure. Its `args` are the model's `by`,
  `time` and `censor`, then the function's own arguments (`time_unit`,
  `x_label`, `y_label`, `legend`).
- `forest_hr`: a forest plot of hazard ratios. It reads the ARD's `HR`
  analysis. Its `args` are its params (`comparison`, `favours` ...).

A report with `figure:` has no `content:`. An unknown name, or a missing
model argument, stops with a message.

```{cat, engine.opts = list(file = file.path(outputs, "F-1.yml"), lang = "yaml")}
id: F-1
kind: figure
label: Overall survival
data:
  - id: adsl_sub
    from: ADSL
    population: ITT
  - id: adtte_sub
    from: ADTTE
    subjects: adsl_sub
    add: [TRT01A]
    where: !r PARAMCD == "OS"
    derive: !r AVAL = AVAL / 30.4375
ard:
  analyses:
    - {id: BIGN, method: categorical, data: adsl_sub, variables: [TRT01A]}
figure:
  name: fig_km
  args:
    by: TRT01A
    time: AVAL
    censor: CNSR
    time_unit: months
    legend: bottom
```

`tfl_content_code()` writes the call:

```{r, opts.label = "code"}
km <- tfl_read_output(file.path(outputs, "F-1.yml"))
cat(tfl_content_code(km), sep = "\n")
```

A forest plot needs only its params:

```yaml
figure:
  name: forest_hr
  args:
    comparison: Drug X
```

`tfl_template_to_spec()` writes this key for the series templates
`tflspec_v1/km_simple` and `tflspec_v1/forest_hr`. `tfl_figure_fn()`
returns the function of a name.

The functions can also be called directly. Here is the call above on the
example data. The legend shows each arm's N from BIGN:

```{r, fig.width = 7, fig.height = 4.5, message = FALSE}
adsl_sub <- adsl[adsl$ITTFL == "Y", ]
adtte_sub <- merge(adtte[adtte$PARAMCD == "OS", setdiff(names(adtte), "TRT01A")],
                   adsl_sub[, c("USUBJID", "TRT01A")], by = "USUBJID")
adtte_sub$AVAL <- adtte_sub$AVAL / 30.4375

ard <- cards::ard_tabulate(adsl_sub, variables = TRT01A)
ard$analysis_id <- "BIGN"

km_fit <- ggsurvfit::survfit2(ggsurvfit::Surv_CNSR(AVAL, CNSR) ~ TRT01A, data = adtte_sub)
fig_km(km_fit, ard = ard, time_unit = "months", legend = "bottom")
```
